messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 50
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Plumber
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Memory: Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing

Vignette:
Kofi, a fifty-year-old plumber with hands that had spent three decades confidently commanding pipes and valves, now sat with those same hands clasped tightly in his lap, a stranger to their former strength. The change, he explained, had begun seven months ago on a routine job in a quiet suburban house. He was under a sink in a basement laundry room, the house empty and still, when the basement door at the top of the stairs creaked open. He’d assumed it was the homeowner returning early, but the footsteps were too heavy, too fast. Before he could fully slide out, two figures were standing over him. The memory of it never came to him as a coherent story he could tell his wife, Amara. Instead, it was a series of silent, vivid pictures: the scuffed toes of their boots, a flash of a face he couldn't quite place, the pattern of the linoleum floor rushing up as he was shoved aside. He couldn’t seem to put the sequence of events into words, the whole encounter feeling like a silent film playing on a loop in his head.

In the weeks that followed, sleep became a foreign country. He would lie awake for hours, his body rigid, listening to the house settle, his mind replaying those frozen images. Each time the picture of him lying helpless on the floor surfaced, a hot wave of guilt would wash over him. He was a big man, strong from years of physical labor, and yet he had done nothing. He had let them take his wallet and a few tools without a fight. This feeling solidified into a painful conviction: he was no longer the man he thought he was, no longer capable of protecting himself or his family. The police report he filed felt like a formality that led nowhere, and the knowledge that the men faced no consequences festered into a deep, burning sense of injustice. The world felt unbalanced, and he felt powerless within it.

This internal erosion began to manifest in his work, the very place that had always defined him. On a job a month after the assault, a client’s teenage son bounded down the basement stairs, and Kofi reacted instantly, dropping a heavy wrench and spinning around with his arms raised. The boy stared, startled, and Kofi felt a shame so profound it was nauseating. After that, any unexpected movement nearby—a door opening, a shadow passing a window—would trigger the same jolt of pure animal terror. He started turning down jobs in unfamiliar neighborhoods or multi-unit buildings where he couldn't control who came and went. His world began to shrink until the only places he felt a sliver of safety were his own home and his workshop in the garage. He began to doubt his every move, questioning whether he’d tightened a fitting enough or if he’d remembered to lock the van, a level of self-doubt he had never experienced in his professional life.

The loss of work put a strain on him and Amara. He saw the worry in her eyes but couldn't explain the fear that now dictated his life. He felt he could no longer trust his own judgment to do the right thing, either on a job or in his life. It was Amara who finally convinced him to seek help, not with anger, but with a quiet plea. "I miss you, Kofi," she had said, her hand on his arm. "I miss the man who believed he could fix anything." He came to therapy not with any real hope, but out of a desperate sense of obligation to her, haunted by the belief that he was fundamentally broken, a man whose capability and confidence had been stolen from him on a cold basement floor.
